newsitem.title: USA: Families of Oklahoma City victims to sue U.S..
newsitem.headline: Families of Oklahoma City victims to sue U.S..

text.p: Families of several Oklahoma City bombing victims Wednesday said they plan to file a multimillion-dollar civil suit against the federal government for allegedly failing to warn of a possible terrorist attack on April 19, 1995.

The families of at least 44 victims alleged the government knew or should have known that federal buildings could be targeted for violent acts on April 19 -- an increasingly significant date among right-wing militia.

Edye Smith, whose two sons were killed in the day-care centre at the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, also said a federal informant had warned the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms that the building had been targeted.

"The government knew there was going to be danger. They should have warned people. I want the government to stand up and say 'Yes, we made a mistake,'" Smith said. "I'm more angry at the government than I am at Timothy McVeigh," she said.

McVeigh is the government's chief suspect in the bombing that killed 168 people and injured hundreds of others. His trial on federal criminal charges is set to open March 31 with jury selection in a Denver courthouse.

The families of the bombing victims said federal agencies should have issued warnings of possible dangers across the country on April 19, the anniversary of a government raid on the Branch Davidian religious compound in Waco, Texas.

Right-wing activist Richard Snell's compound in Arkansas was raided on the same date in 1985 and Snell was executed on that date in 1995 in Louisiana hours before a truck bomb ripped apart the Murrah building in downtown Oklahoma City, the families said.

Right-wing activists had issued a "call to arms" ahead of Snell's execution that the families allege went unheeded by federal agencies including the FBI, ATF, General Services Administration and Federal Protective Services.

Connecticut attorney Richard Bieder, who is representing the families, said not all of them believe there was advance warning of the attack. But he said the government "could or should have done more than it did, particularly in Oklahoma City, if not in other jurisdictions."
He said each family taking part in the suit plans to ask for $25 million in damages. The families face a two-year statute of limitations on April 19 for filing claims against the government.
